progressionInfo.name: I-V Progression
progressionInfo.subtitle: The simplest and most powerful chord pairing in music - a two-chord pattern built on dominant tension and tonic resolution that drives punk rock, folk, and countless campfire singalongs.

properties.label: I (Tonic)
properties.value: Home base, stability, the point of rest

properties.label: V (Dominant)
properties.value: Maximum tension, strongest pull back to tonic

properties.label: Relationship
properties.value: The simplest tension-resolution cycle in harmony

properties.label: Interval
properties.value: Root movement of a perfect fifth (or fourth)

properties.label: Why It Works
properties.value: The dominant chord contains the leading tone that resolves to the tonic root

examples.label: Leading Tone
examples.value: F# in D major resolves up to G

chordDiagrams.title: I-V in G Major
practiceNotes: These two chords are among the easiest open shapes
Focus on quick, clean transitions between G and D
Try alternating every 2 beats, then every beat
Listen for the pull from D back to G

chordDiagrams.title: I-V in E Major
chordDiagrams.description: Using B7 as a common open-position substitute for B major:
practiceNotes: B7 is the standard open-position voicing for the V chord in E
The added b7 (A) strengthens the pull back to E
Great key for blues and rock riffs

advancedApplications.title: Common Variations
advancedApplications.description: Ways to expand the I-V framework:
items: I-V-V-I (extended dominant before resolution)
I-V-I-V (steady alternation, great for verses)
I-V7 (add the 7th for stronger pull)
I5-V5 (power chord version for punk and rock)
I-V with bass pedal (keep root in bass throughout)

advancedApplications.title: Key Transposition
items: C Major: C - G
D Major: D - A
E Major: E - B (or B7)
A Major: A - E
G Major: G - D

advancedApplications.title: Rhythm & Strumming Ideas
advancedApplications.description: Two chords means rhythm carries the song:
items: Driving eighth-note strums for punk energy
Boom-chick alternating bass for country feel
Syncopated upstroke pattern for reggae influence
Palm-muted power chords for heavy rock
Fingerpicked arpeggios for folk ballads

notatedExercises.title: Exercise 1: Basic I-V Alternation
notatedExercises.description: Practice the fundamental two-chord change in G major:
practiceNotes: Hold each chord for 4 beats (whole notes)
Focus on clean, immediate chord changes
Listen for the tension on D resolving to G

notatedExercises.description: Fast eighth-note power chord changes in E:
practiceNotes: Use downstrokes only for authentic punk feel
Palm mute for tighter, punchier sound

sections.title: Scale Degrees
items: I (G): 1st degree - Tonic, point of rest
V (D): 5th degree - Dominant, point of tension
Root movement by perfect 5th (G to D)
Strongest harmonic relationship in tonal music
Foundation for all other progressions

sections.title: Why V Resolves to I
items: The V chord contains the leading tone (7th scale degree)
Leading tone is a half step below the tonic
This half-step pull creates the sensation of resolution
Adding a 7th to V (V7) strengthens the pull further

sections.title: Common Tones (G and D major)
items: G major (G-B-D) and D major (D-F#-A)
D is the common tone between both chords
B moves down to A (whole step)
G moves to F# (half step) or leaps to A
F# (leading tone) resolves up to G

sections.title: The Dominant-Tonic Axis
items: I and V are the two most important chords in any key
Every cadence ultimately relies on V to I motion
The authentic cadence (V-I) is the strongest resolution
All other progressions elaborate on this fundamental relationship
